27-11.title: Check your maternity cover before pregnancy: ESIC, PM-JAY or a state scheme may pay for the delivery
27-11.inPlainWords: India has no single maternity insurance for everyone. An insured worker under ESIC gets maternity benefit and medical care; an eligible household under PM-JAY gets hospital cover; some states run a maternity scheme. A private policy may have a waiting period. Check the cover, the empanelled hospital and the documents before you conceive, not during labour.
27-11.benefit: The ESIC maternity benefit includes a cash benefit for the insured woman and medical treatment. PM-JAY covers maternity and newborn care for eligible households at empanelled hospitals. The Pradhan Mantri Matru Vandana Yojana gives a cash benefit to an eligible woman for the first living child. A private health policy may cover maternity after a waiting period. The National Health Mission runs free delivery services at public facilities.
27-11.cost: ESIC and PM-JAY are contribution or eligibility based; a public facility is free. A private policy's premium and waiting period apply.
27-11.caveats: A policy bought after conception may exclude the pregnancy. A cashless claim needs pre-authorisation. Keep the antenatal records and the scheme card.
27-11.sources: Employees' State Insurance Corporation. <https://esic.gov.in/>; National Health Authority, PM-JAY. <https://nha.gov.in/>; Ministry of Women and Child Development, PMMVY. <https://wcd.gov.in/>; Ministry of Health and Family Welfare. <https://mohfw.gov.in/>

27-12.title: Get the birth registered and the certificate early; the hospital gives the birth report and the registrar issues the certificate
27-12.inPlainWords: The hospital reports the birth to the local registrar under the Registration of Births and Deaths Act, 1969, and the family can apply for the birth certificate. Register within 21 days to avoid a late fee. Decide the baby's name before the registration if the state requires it. The birth certificate is needed for the Aadhaar, the school admission and the passport.
27-12.benefit: The 1969 Act requires the birth to be registered within 21 days; a late registration needs the registrar's permission and a fee. The hospital issues a birth report, and the municipal registrar issues the certificate. A name can be added later in some states. The certificate is the basis for the Aadhaar enrolment and the school record.
27-12.cost: The registration fee is small; a late fee applies after 21 days.
27-12.caveats: Check the spelling of the name and the parents' details before you leave the registrar. A correction needs an affidavit and a fee. Do not pay an agent to 'fast-track' a birth certificate.
27-12.sources: Registration of Births and Deaths Act, 1969. <https://www.indiacode.nic.in/>; Ministry of Home Affairs, civil registration. <https://crsorgi.gov.in/>; Unique Identification Authority of India. <https://uidai.gov.in/>

27-14.title: Add the newborn to your health cover early: PM-JAY or ESIC can cover the baby without waiting for Aadhaar
27-14.inPlainWords: A newborn can be covered under PM-JAY or ESIC as a dependant, usually without an Aadhaar of their own. The mother's card and the birth certificate are enough for the initial enrolment; the Aadhaar can be added later. Do not wait for the birth registration to be complete before you ask the scheme office. A delay can leave the baby uninsured for the first weeks.
27-14.benefit: PM-JAY covers the newborn as part of the eligible household, and the scheme's guidelines allow enrolment with the mother's card and the birth record. ESIC covers the insured person's dependants, including a newborn. The National Health Mission's public facilities provide newborn care. The Aadhaar is not mandatory for a newborn's emergency treatment.
27-14.cost: PM-JAY is free for an eligible household. ESIC is contribution based.
27-14.caveats: The enrolment process differs by state. A private policy may have a waiting period for a newborn. Keep the birth certificate and the mother's card.
27-14.sources: National Health Authority, PM-JAY. <https://nha.gov.in/>; Employees' State Insurance Corporation. <https://esic.gov.in/>; Ministry of Health and Family Welfare. <https://mohfw.gov.in/>

27-15.title: Register the birth with the municipal registrar within 21 days — not at a police station
27-15.inPlainWords: A birth is registered with the local municipal registrar under the Registration of Births and Deaths Act, 1969, not with the police. The hospital usually reports the birth; the family applies for the certificate. If the birth is at home, the family must report it to the registrar. Register within 21 days to avoid a late fee and a longer process.
27-15.benefit: The 1969 Act requires registration within 21 days. The hospital's birth report and the parents' identity proof are the main documents. A late registration needs the registrar's permission and a fee. The certificate is required for the Aadhaar, the school admission and the passport. A police station has no role in a normal birth registration.
27-15.cost: The fee is small; a late fee applies after 21 days.
27-15.caveats: A home birth needs a witness and a medical certificate where available. Check the name spelling. A correction needs an affidavit.
27-15.sources: Registration of Births and Deaths Act, 1969. <https://www.indiacode.nic.in/>; Ministry of Home Affairs, civil registration. <https://crsorgi.gov.in/>; Unique Identification Authority of India. <https://uidai.gov.in/>

27-2.title: Register the pregnancy early: get the MCP card, book the antenatal visits, and ask about PMSMA, JSY and PM-JAY
27-2.inPlainWords: Register as soon as you know you are pregnant, at the sub-centre, the primary health centre or the health-and-wellness centre, or with the ASHA worker for your area. You will be given a Mother and Child Protection card, which records every visit and test. The national programme expects at least four antenatal visits with the first in the first trimester, and the World Health Organization now recommends eight contacts. The Pradhan Mantri Surakshit Matritva Abhiyan offers a free check-up on the ninth of every month at a government facility, and delivery at a public facility is free.
27-2.benefit: The National Health Mission runs antenatal care through the sub-centre, the primary health centre and the health-and-wellness centre, with the MCP card as the record and the ASHA worker as the link. PMSMA gives a fixed-day free antenatal check-up, the Janani Suraksha Yojana gives a cash incentive to an eligible mother who delivers at a public facility, and PM-JAY covers maternity at an empanelled hospital for an eligible household. Early registration is what makes the anaemia, blood pressure, sugar and infection checks happen in time.
27-2.cost: Care at a public facility is free, including the tests in the national programme. A private hospital charges its own fee.
27-2.caveats: Carry the MCP card to every visit and keep it after the delivery. A private hospital may not accept a public-scheme card, so ask before you book. Do not skip a visit because you feel well.
27-2.sources: National Health Mission, maternal health. <https://nhm.gov.in/>; Ministry of Health and Family Welfare. <https://www.mohfw.gov.in/>; National Health Authority, PM-JAY. <https://nha.gov.in/>

27-3.title: Test for HIV, syphilis and hepatitis B at the first antenatal visit: the tests and the treatment are free in the public programme
27-3.inPlainWords: At your first antenatal visit, ask for an HIV test, a syphilis test and a hepatitis B test. In the public system the HIV test is done at an Integrated Counselling and Testing Centre, free and confidential, and if it is positive the programme that prevents transmission from mother to child provides the medicines and follows the baby. Syphilis is tested and treated free, and the hepatitis B birth dose is part of the routine immunisation schedule. Tell the doctor if you were tested somewhere else, so the record is complete.
27-3.benefit: The National AIDS Control Programme runs the testing centres and the programme that gives a pregnant woman and her baby free antiretroviral treatment. The National Viral Hepatitis Control Programme provides free testing and treatment for hepatitis B and C, and the universal immunisation programme gives a hepatitis B birth dose. Treating syphilis in pregnancy prevents congenital syphilis. In all three infections, treatment during pregnancy is what changes the outcome for the child.
27-3.cost: Free at a government testing centre and a public antenatal clinic. A private laboratory charges its own rate.
27-3.caveats: Show a test done at a private laboratory to the antenatal clinic. A negative test early in pregnancy may need a repeat if there is a later risk. Do not delay the first visit in order to have the test.
27-3.sources: National AIDS Control Organisation. <https://naco.gov.in/>; Ministry of Health and Family Welfare. <https://www.mohfw.gov.in/>; National Health Mission. <https://nhm.gov.in/>

27-8.title: If your waters break, lie down and call an ambulance at once — 108 or 112 — and do not wait at home
27-8.inPlainWords: If your waters break, lie down on your left side where you are and call 108 for an ambulance, or 112 for the emergency response service, straight away. Do not walk around, do not take a bath, and do not wait to see whether labour starts. The danger is a prolapsed cord, where the cord comes down before the baby and the baby's oxygen is cut off; that needs a hospital within minutes. Note the time the waters broke and the colour of the fluid, and tell the doctor.
27-8.benefit: A prolapsed cord is an obstetric emergency: the mother is positioned to take pressure off the cord and the baby is delivered urgently, usually by caesarean. India's emergency number is 112 for police, fire and ambulance, and 108 reaches a free emergency ambulance in most states. Getting to a facility that can do a caesarean is the priority, which is why the call comes before the bag is packed.
27-8.cost: A 108 ambulance is free in most states. A private ambulance charges, and the delivery may be free at a public facility.
27-8.caveats: Do not take a bath or a shower after the waters break. Do not wait for contractions. If the cord is visible, do not push it back in: lie down and call.
27-8.sources: Ministry of Health and Family Welfare. <https://www.mohfw.gov.in/>; National Health Mission. <https://nhm.gov.in/>; Ministry of Home Affairs, Emergency Response Support System. <https://www.mha.gov.in/>

27-9.title: Ask for labour analgesia: an epidural is given on request, and it does not make a caesarean more likely
27-9.inPlainWords: An epidural is the most effective pain relief in labour, and it does not increase the chance of a caesarean section; the claim that it causes lasting back pain is not supported by the evidence. In India it is offered at many private hospitals and at some government medical colleges, but not everywhere, because an anaesthetist has to be available. Ask at an antenatal visit rather than in the middle of a contraction, and put it in your birth plan. There is no national price: the hospital sets the charge and often bills it separately.
27-9.benefit: An epidural blocks the pain of labour while the mother stays awake and can push. The evidence does not show that it raises the caesarean rate, although it can lengthen the second stage a little. Availability depends on the anaesthetist and the hospital, so asking early is the practical step. If the hospital does not offer it, ask what else it can give.
27-9.cost: The hospital sets the fee, usually separate from the delivery package. A public hospital may charge little or nothing, or may not offer it at all.
27-9.caveats: An epidural is not suitable for every woman: a clotting problem, an infection at the site or a low platelet count may rule it out. It is placed by an anaesthetist with monitoring. Do not accept a bare refusal without asking the reason.
27-9.sources: Ministry of Health and Family Welfare, maternal health. <https://www.mohfw.gov.in/>; National Health Mission. <https://nhm.gov.in/>

27-13.title: Do not skip newborn screening: India has no universal national programme, so ask what your hospital actually offers
27-13.inPlainWords: India does not run a universal newborn screening programme for every baby. Some states and some hospitals screen for congenital hypothyroidism, congenital adrenal hyperplasia, G6PD deficiency and hearing loss, and many do not. Ask the hospital before the delivery what it screens and what it charges, and ask again after the birth. If a test is not done, a hearing test and a developmental check are available through the Rashtriya Bal Swasthya Karyakram and its district early intervention centre, and a doctor can order a thyroid test if there is a concern.
27-13.benefit: Newborn screening finds a condition before the symptoms appear, when treatment still prevents the damage, and congenital hypothyroidism is the clearest example. The Rashtriya Bal Swasthya Karyakram screens children for the four Ds, including hearing, and refers a positive case to a district early intervention centre. Because there is no national mandate, the decision sits with the hospital and the parents, which is exactly why you should ask instead of assuming.
27-13.cost: A private hospital charges for its screening panel. A test in a public programme is free where it is offered.
27-13.caveats: Not done is not the same as normal. If the baby was not screened and there is poor feeding, jaundice or a delayed milestone, see a paediatrician. Keep the screening card with the immunisation record.
27-13.sources: Ministry of Health and Family Welfare, child health. <https://www.mohfw.gov.in/>; National Health Mission, Rashtriya Bal Swasthya Karyakram. <https://nhm.gov.in/>

27-16.title: Do not skip the postpartum check: six weeks after birth is when anaemia, infection and depression are found
27-16.inPlainWords: Under the Home Based Newborn Care programme an ASHA worker visits the mother and the baby on set days in the first six weeks, and the mother should also be seen at a facility at about six weeks. That visit is where anaemia, raised blood pressure, an infection, a wound that is not healing and postpartum depression are picked up. India does not fund a universal free six-week check-up the way some systems do, but the visit is available at a government facility, and the delivery and follow-up may be covered by JSY or PM-JAY. Ask for the depression screening.
27-16.benefit: The home-visit schedule runs through the first 42 days and covers the mother's health and the baby's feeding and weight. Postpartum depression is common and treatable: the Tele-MANAS helpline on 14416 gives free mental-health support, and a district hospital has a psychiatrist. Anaemia and high blood pressure after delivery can worsen silently. The six-week visit is also the point to discuss contraception and the spacing of the next pregnancy.
27-16.cost: A public facility visit is free. A private consultation is charged, and Tele-MANAS is free.
27-16.caveats: Do not assume that feeling low is normal and will pass. Do not stop the iron tablets without asking. Take the MCP card and the discharge summary to the visit.
27-16.sources: National Health Mission, Home Based Newborn Care. <https://nhm.gov.in/>; Ministry of Health and Family Welfare, Tele-MANAS. <https://www.mohfw.gov.in/>; National Health Authority. <https://nha.gov.in/>

27-1.cost: Folic acid tablets are cheap, and at government health centres they are usually supplied free as part of antenatal care. The real challenge is remembering to take one pill every day.

27-5.cost: Low‑dose aspirin is inexpensive and widely stocked, and public antenatal clinics generally supply it without charge when it is prescribed. One tablet per day must be taken until delivery. The hard part is remembering to take it every single day.

27-6.cost: Cost depends on where the test is done: public antenatal clinics include it in routine care, while private laboratories bill separately. You must fast beforehand, and several blood draws will take up half a morning.
